On one occasion I was called directly by President Izetbegovic and at the time he said "Vaha, what are the members of the 9th Brigade doing over there?" I think he said also directly, "What is Ramiz Delalic doing?" I replied, "I don't know what they are doing. What are they doing? Can you please tell me?" "Well, you go and see what's going on. They are walking up and down these streets and going in these buildings and is it true that they are taking money through racketeering?" So I instructed the security service to do -- to start an investigation, but there was no argumented evidence ultimately. So perhaps this corresponds to this part of the 21st of December 1992. As far as the 28th December is concerned is something that I hadn't heard of and cannot confirm. The next paragraph is also on the same date. I didn't hear anything about it and cannot confirm it. January 1st, 1993? Specifically, this vehicle, this PUCH, is something that I did not hear about, but I did have information that from time to time, some types of vehicles were seized or taken from someone. Whether it was from socially owned companies and organisations or from individuals. This is in the context of January 1st, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's by Ramiz Delalic, the seizure? The seizure was by Ramiz Delalic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said you did hear about -- you did have information that vehicles were seized or taken from someone. Taken by whom? Was it Ramiz Delalic? Is that what you're saying? Or his men?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that came most frequently would say members of the 9th Motorised Brigade. After that, public opinion would be formed. Whatever was not good in the 9th Motorised Brigade, you would immediately think of Ramiz Delalic, Celo, regardless of whether he was really responsible for that or not. So it's possible but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Flex one, 10th of February 1993. I'm sorry, there is also a -- before that, there is a meeting chaired by Ramiz in which he rudely attacked the political and military leadership of the country.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I seem to vaguely remember some of that. However, I cannot confirm it. The 10th of February 1993, I cannot confirm anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 23rd of March, Delalic and three armed persons threatening the owner of the delta catering establishment in Breka requesting 4.000 Deutschmarks, which they eventually got.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was information of this sort, but at the same time, what it states here in the past age referring to the 23rd of March is something that I'm hearing for the first time, actually now that I've read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Next one is the 28th of March, the seizure of a freight motor vehicle at Bradina, when Delalic's unit was at Mount Igman. They were committing criminal acts and violations of discipline on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the stay at Igman, the units of the 9th Motorised Brigade and Ramiz Delalic, there was some information about them, but it wasn't so much that the information was about him. It was more about Caco. That's a fact. The 11th of May 1993. There was information from time to time with his quarrels with the civilian police, so perhaps this would correspond to what it states here for the 11th of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 26th of -- sorry, 29th of June 1993, a raid on a cafe ordering the cafe owner to pay 9.000 Deutschmarks a month to him, and then ordering all the customers and staff to be taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 7th of July 1993, two members of the brigade throwing a hand grenade into number 33 Sekerova street, killing Hadziba Humic and wounding seven people.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember vaguely that there was some bomb throwing by members of the 9th Motorised Brigade in some street in the town, but I don't know whether that is this specific incident when these people were killed. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 24th of July, 1993. The seizure of eight bullet proof vests from local and foreign journalists, that's Reuters and other press agencies.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is what I recollect the best, because I think I was also involved to a certain extent in the return of those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Next one, the 1st of August, 1993, Delalic firing a gun at the back glass of a vehicle driven by Boris Krstanovic, Cile.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he did this shooting, because there was shooting. There was constant shooting in Sarajevo, and I don't want to be funny, but sometimes you didn't know who was shooting at whom. But this refers to what I was explaining about the conflict between the 9th Motorised unit held by Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and Boris Krstanovic, Cile, who was the commander of the sabotage unit in front of the corps command when I personally, with the corps commander, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, prevented this conflict. This corresponds to that incident. These are their mutual clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 2nd of August 1993, surrounding by five armed soldiers of a Land Rover containing 4 BBC journalists, holding them at gun point seizing their bullet proof vests and a significant amount of US dollars. And so on.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this. Perhaps I'm mixing this up with the previous incident with the bullet proof vests. I'm not sure. I'm not quite clear whether it's the same thing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 17th of August, 1993. Members of the 9th Motorised Brigade military police searching apartments in Cvijetina street looking for fuel. 1

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 23rd of August 1993, Celo and 20 members of the brigade assaulting Ramiz Patura [phoen] of the 4th Motorised Brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. These are quite minor incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 25th of August, 1993. 9th Brigade military police bringing in Adija Mulahalilovic [phoen], brother of the owner of the Bakara [phoen] cafe, and seizing 2.000 Deutschmarks by force from him and being forced to sign a "contract of donorship" for 50 Deutschmarks a week.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is derived from those general reports given to the chief, which I saw from time to time, but I really cannot confirm this incident. The same thing can be said for the next incident also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. There is a number of other incidents mentioned. Can you just briefly tell us if you can confirm any of the other ones? And that's the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I really don't know all the documents that are in the -- all the incidents that are in this document. I've talked about some of them. Most of these incidents mentioned, the place names, and specific names. I don't know where each cafe is or the names of the persons involved. I am seeing most of these incidents in this document for the first time and I'm wondering myself whether this is all true or not, and if it's true -- if it's true, that's not good, but if it's not true, that's not good either, all the more so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I want to move from that document. What -- what was your involvement in Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the Trebevic operation, I was the commander of the 1st Corps, Bakir Alispahic was the minister for internal affairs, the minister of the civilian police. General Rasim Delic was the commander of the Supreme Command Staff. A document signed by President Izetbegovic, as far as I can remember, the Minister of Internal Affairs and the Supreme Command Staff, the civilian police were assigned, as well as people from the 1st Corps, to carry out this task. The operation was prepared. On the 26th in the morning at around 4 a.m., I think the armed combat began. The names of the people that I mentioned, this team, was formed. It was a coordination team, which was located in the centre of old town, Stari Grad, and this is more or less the location between the 9th and the 10th brigades. In front of me, in front of my command, I sent my deputy Ismet Dahic to represent me in that team. Kemo Arnautovic was there representing the minister of internal affairs, and so on and so forth and another group of officers because we were all linked up into a unified communication chain and command chain. The operation began in the morning. It was planned to last for two days, most probably, but more or less the operation was brought to a close on that same day, late at night, around midnight or after midnight, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many units were involved in Operation Trebevic? And what was the numerical strength of those who were engaged in Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at my main command post the whole time, and I commanded and controlled all the units directly with my deputy. It's hard to say exactly how many units participated. I could -- I would have to refresh my memory by looking at documents. I think that practically all of the brigades that I trusted 100 per cent, let's say, that they would not betray me, not in the sense of the brigade as such but in terms of the officers in that brigade, commanders of the brigades, of the battalions and so on. So from five, six or seven brigades, I took an average of a battalion that was specially formed over the previous 15 or 20 days during the preparations for the operation, and on the 25th, 26th of October 1993, I issued the tasks and at the same time, even the direct participants in the operation did not know exactly what they would be doing, and I did not tell them this because I was concerned that this information could be leaked and the operation could fail, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Numbers, numbers, figures.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 5.000 men in the encirclement of the command posts, commands, and officers of the 9th and 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was it directed at? Trebevic. What was its aim?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now talking about this part of the Trebevic operation, which in some elements had also broader context. The part that I'm talking about was aimed at eliminating Musan Topalovic, Caco, and Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and all of their followers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why was it considered necessary to employ 5.000 men to do that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had to ensure considerable superiority in strength in relation to the estimated number of soldiers who could, at a certain point in time, decide to stand by Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there fighting?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite fierce fighting. Whether we are talking about the 10th Mountain Brigade and Caco. However, when we talking about the 9th motorised and Ramiz Delalic, Celo, we did not have serious fighting in his case because he acted wisely. He surrendered. He didn't kill anyone. His soldiers did not kill anyone either. Whereas on the other side, Caco and his followers killed about 15 people, I think, soldiers. And in particular, four military police officers from my military police and four civilian police officers from civilian police, including amongst those four civilian police officers who took part in that operation the son of minister Avdo Hebib was killed. And excuse me, when we are talking about this, at that point in time, I'm not sure whether it was Avdo Hebib or Bakir Alispahic who were minister of internal affairs. I'm not sure about that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why was it considered necessary to eliminate Caco and Celo and all of their followers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that enough was said already so far, in order to establish a unified chain of command in the 1st Corps of the Army of Republika Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you have to undertake military means? Why couldn't it have been done by other means?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was very difficult to do this by other means, most probably, and the political side decided to do it like that. I could not go into action without a political decision, and without a decision of the Supreme Command, because I was aware that if I did not have political support for any military operation, that military operation would be doomed to fail in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber earlier that there were disciplinary problems within other brigades and some instances of criminality. Was action -- this military action taken against them or was it confined to the 9th and the 10th?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say to establish a unified chain of command in the 1st Corps, that's why the action was undertaken. So along with eliminating the people and the groups of those people, we would also eliminate all of these things that we read about in the previous document which numbers 13 pages, because probably the political side finally decided that this cannot be confirmed. But they could not deal with all of these accumulated problems either, which they were encountering. These problems were being hyperproduced and in order to prevent these alleged crimes by Musan Topalovic, Caco, and the racketeering, and along with that, in accordance with certain information, committed by Ramiz Delalic, Celo, as well. That's why the operation was initiated, Not only because of Caco and Celo. A month later, an armed action was carried out against a brigade, the Croatian brigade, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The other brigades you mentioned yesterday in your testimony, in which there were disciplinary or criminal problems, was military action taken against them at the same time? Was it confined to the 9th and the 10th? If it wasn't taken against the others, why not? Why was it confined to the 9th and the 10th, if it was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find the question far too general. It depended on the extent of the problem involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you said you needed 5.000 men to go in against the 9th and the 10th. That was a military action. Did you take similar military action, armed soldiers and fighting, against the other brigades in which there were disciplinary or criminal problems, apart from the HVO one a month later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think -- the witness didn't say HVO, I think he said the Croatian unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was a completely unintentional lapse. I meant the Croat unit, Croat doesn't necessarily mean HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made a mistake. It was the brigade of the Croatian Defence Council. I made a mistake when I said a Croatian brigade. What I said was about the Croatian Defence Council brigade in Sarajevo that was there. After that, some other armed actions were taken against certain commanders in Sarajevo. Not to that extent. To a far lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that Celo surrendered but Caco didn't. Did you get to see both of those men during the operation? I don't -- I want the short version of this, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they brought to your office?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As agreed, if I can put it that way, although it is not for me to seek any kind of agreement with my superiors, but when this action was planned, it was said that if anybody is taken prisoner, especially those two men, that they would be taken to the Supreme Command, to the staff of the Supreme Command, or, rather, to the Supreme Command, President Izetbegovic. That's the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question was, were they brought to your office?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One at a time or together?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who came first?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It's not that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's talk about Celo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I beg your pardon, first Ramiz Delalic, Celo, came, or rather he was brought in by the military police, the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he under arrest?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a result of your speaking to him, was he taken elsewhere and detained, taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I finished speaking to him, I asked the security service to have him handcuffed in my office, and I ordered the security service to take him to prison, that he should be taken into custody, and then the relevant proceedings were supposed to be initiated. That is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now Caco, was he brought to your office under arrest?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him too?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he likewise leave your office in handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was he on his way to when he left your office? And who was he with?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it your --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From me, he was sent to the same person -- same place to where Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was sent, to the Viktor Bubanj barracks. That's where he was sent. Or Ramiz Sultan [phoen] barracks. When he left the corps on his way to the prison, somewhere along the way he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying he didn't make it to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know on whose orders he was liquidated or how he was liquidated?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, that's the question that's been bandied about for the past ten years and no one has an answer to that. So neither do I on this occasion, before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You said that Mr. -- sorry, Delalic was to be taken into custody and relevant proceedings were supposed to be initiated. My questions now are about military -- the system of military discipline. I want some fairly short answers if possible. Was there a district military court operating in Sarajevo at that time, August, September, October, 1993? It's really a yes or no answer, if you can possibly confine it to that, because I will then ask you other questions.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me yes or no. It kept changing all the time. The first courts were transformed into the second courts and then the second courts were transformed into the first courts. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, was there a court, however styled, of the district military court operating in Sarajevo in that period?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is beyond my competence. I don't want to go into all of that. Legal people know that best of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were cases of criminality by soldiers in the 1st Corps referred to a district military court in Sarajevo in the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question whether I had any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 1st Corps. You were the commander. Do you know of cases?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Being referred to a district military court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was the Court dealing with these cases that were referred there by the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there other district military courts operating or functioning in the territory held by the Federation in that same period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to this. The Prosecutor took a deliberate decision not to call the person who could answer these questions, clearly. There witness has indicated that he's not comfortable in answering questions about this area of competence. I have to put it on the record, as I did last time, that this happened, that when the Prosecution deliberately makes a decision, frankly in cold blood, not to call a particular witness, and then seeks to get this material, I have to object. Your Honours overruled me on this one before I have to say but I have to place it on the record, and I do make the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's not engage in pointing fingers with each other at this stage. Well, I believe that this question is the natural course from the previous questions. I believe that Mr. Re is entitled to ask these questions. It depends on the witness how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is were there other district military courts functioning in the territory held by the Federation in that -- in that period?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it functioning?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say now that when preparing my military expertise for the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case, that inter alia I partly touched upon that question too. There was such a court. However, it had enormous problems on different grounds, in terms of its functioning. And among other things, what was proven was, if I can refer to it now, it was burdened with a great many cases from the commander of the 3rd Corps and they didn't manage to do their part of the job with regard to these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a court in Tuzla functioning?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a court functioning in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established with a bit of a delay but the answer is yes again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mostar and Tuzla are concerned, I'm not too sure, but they should have been there. Now, I cannot make any assertions in terms of whether there was or whether there wasn't. Or in Konjic, I don't know. I don't know. I do not know. I cannot confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D146.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the inspection team order of the 30th of August 1993. Now, first of all, what, in military terms, in Bosnia, in the Bosnian army in 1993, was an inspection team?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question which is directly and 100 per cent suited for an expert. However, I can speak in general terms and in terms of principle. When we say inspection, that means that we are talking about inspection when one says inspection or inspection team, which is one and the same thing, according to the customary rules or mode of operating and what I know from the Yugoslav People's Army that I originally came from, and in accordance with the fact that we practically inherited all the documents of the Yugoslav People's Army or regulations to the largest extent, inspection is a body or organ established by, say, specifically, or rather in most cases, the highest command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our case, it was the staff of the Supreme Command or the General Staff or even the Supreme Command, or outside the military, the Ministry of Defence can also set up an inspection. Once an inspection is established, then its composition is determined, its timing, and it is given precise tasks and instructions, depending on the type of task for which an inspection is established, appropriate profiles of officers are sought who would serve on the said inspection team. It is then directly responsible to the top military authority or the Ministry of Defence, if they set up the inspection. That is one thing. And another matter is the following: An inspection can have practically all the powers of the body that establishes it; however, the body that establishes the inspection most frequently restricts the scope of that inspection according to certain matters, and so on and so forth. I tried to give you the key elements, as far as inspection is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can an inspection team be authorised to engage in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to make a mistake. An inspection team -- I mean, the word "inspection" itself denotes the inspecting of something. That means that it can have the right to inspect combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about to direct or command combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as commanding combat activities is concerned, the chain has to be somewhat clearer. Although in the army, everything has to be clear, let us be clear on that. That's the way it should be, although it is not always. However, I can just repeat this particular word yet again. Everything depends on what the concrete case involved is. And I is a see that we are discussing a concrete case. What Rasim Delic, the head of staff of the Supreme Command, gave to General Sefer Halilovic, in terms of authority as head of the inspection team, did he give him every thought or did he restrict his authority? This is related to the sentence I gave you in response to the general question about inspections as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we could just have a look at the document, D146, I want you to give your opinion as a person who was at the time the commander of one corps, as to what that order authorise s the inspection team to do.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was clear. All the authority that the person establishing -- the person or body establishing the inspection team has can be vested in the inspection team. So if the staff of the Supreme Command establishes an inspection team, if they so wish, they can give or he, rather, as head of the staff of the Supreme Command, can vest all his authority in the inspection team. As I've already said, that is usually not the case, to give absolutely all authority to the inspection team, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking about --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking about this document. I want you to read this document and I want you to read order 1, where it says "the team's main assignments are." And the next sentence. And particularly the use of the word "rukovodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also saw this document once I came here. That is to say I hadn't seen it before, and I read it. As for these four items under paragraph 1, it says what the certain powers vested in the team are. In item 1, where the first dash is, "viewing the combat readiness of the commands and units, specifically in the field," and the last part of that sentence is, "And directing combat operations". So, of course, this is the 4th and 6th Corps that is referred to as in the previous text. And directing is a higher level than command and control, but you cannot translate that into English. So there cannot be a proper distinction between the two words in the English language. In Bosnian, there can be that kind of distinction. This word "directing," which is in this document, is stronger and more all-embracing than the word "command and control." Command is part of this word, rukovodjenje. Now, the second item, where the second dash is. "Assessing the resources and forces available and their use accordingly." The second sentence stems from the first sentence. Now, the third item, "resolving personnel problems and logistic support in all segments." As a soldier, if any expert would be brought in, I mean, this question, resolving personnel issues, those who set up an inspection team most often say "I give all authority to the inspection team except for..." and then he usually keeps finance for himself so that the inspection team cannot overspend. And also that the inspection team cannot have personnel moved around. However, here, in item 2, or item 3, we see that this inspection team can resolve personnel issues and logistical issues and so on. Now, the 4th item, of course, being derived from all the above-mentioned, it relates to an overview of the functioning of civilian authorities and bringing them in line with the needs of the armed struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want you to comment on is just going back to the first one, where you said that "directing is a higher level than command and control," but you can't translate it into English. What, in a practical sense, do you mean by directing is a higher level than command and control? What does that mean in a practical sense, that the team is authorised to do?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower the level is of the military structure, let me be most clear. The section is the lowest military formation. Then we have the platoon and then the company. In these lowest military structures and formations, there is practically no direction. There is only command, because the squad or platoon commander directly orders the soldier to do such and such a task, period. And there is practically nothing of this other element of direction. And then, as the level of the structure gets higher, the brigade, battalion, operative group, corps, army, as we get up the chain, the category of command is lower and the part of direction or control increases. So at the higher levels of the military structure, the term "command" is less present, where the term of "direction" or "control" is present much more. But one cannot go without the other. It would be very hard. They go together. That's why you have this term "command and control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, I believe that it's time for a break. Otherwise, the tape will run out. And we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Going back to D146 which is the inspection team document and the answer you gave just before the break, you were talking about direction and command and control. In real terms, what does this authorise the inspection team to do in relation to combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say anything else about the last part of the sentence in item 1, and direction or control, control of combat activities. That term speaks for itself, if we are talking about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does that on its face authorise the inspection team to initiate combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are just details now, which can include what you say, but they don't have to. It all depends on the direct mutual contact between those who set up the inspection team and the leader of the inspection team. In this case, since we are talking about this document, it depends on the communication between General Rasim Delic and General Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about an operation -- about operations groups, and just as briefly as you possibly can, tell the Trial Chamber what an operations group was.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations groups were often used in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Operation groups as a term are not used for the first time in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but were inherited from the doctrinal guidelines of the Yugoslav People's Army. What is an operations group? Namely, as opposed to structures in the army, the organisational establishment structures from the lowest such structure, squad, then platoon, company, battalion, regiment, division, corps, army, and so on and so forth, which are permanent. It's very important, this word, permanent establishment structures. An operations group, which is placed as an equal of a division, because in the English language, there is no special word that can differentiate the words "divizija" and "divizion." These are two different things, even though the same word is used for them. If we use the word "divizion," it's a unit, the rank of a battalion, but it's an artillery unit. I'm not thinking of that unit. I'm thinking of the term "divizija," division, a larger unit, which can number up to 10.000 soldiers. So an operations group would be equal to that division, which can number up to 10.000 soldiers on average, from five to 10.000. An operations group, as opposed to all of these other organisational establishment structures in an army, is not a permanent structure, but a provisional one, and I'm ending on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. What typically what functions did an operations group perform? Why were they set up? What were their tasks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operations group more or less has the same functions as the division command. The command of the operations group would be the same as the division command. It doesn't have all the services, however, all the organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are they used for combat, specific combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who commands an operations group? And how is the command appointed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way as the commanders of other permanent structures and establishments, the same as the brigade commander. The operations group commander would be appointed in the same way that a battalion or a brigade commander would be appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is an operations group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment, sorry, excuse me. Your Honours, I object to this. Your Honours it has to be clarified by the Prosecution, is it now set to be part of there case that there was an operations group in existence here? And we can't have this just drifting along. We need this to be clearly enunciated now. The Prosecution is seeking to add this as part of their case, that there was an operations group and that it's relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I reminds my learned friend of our opening in which we said this was tantamount to an operations group. It wasn't called one but its structure and purpose was tantamount to an operations group. Of course, Mr. Morrissey, I do recall, cross-examined I can't recall which witness now, but a witness I took as an operations group and who set them up, was it the president or the chief of the -- commander of the -- of the -- sorry, the Supreme Commander. So it is an issue in the trial, so yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean that the inspection team, in your view, is the -- is an operational group?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's tantamount to it. It has the same functions as an operations group, it does have a different name. We opened on that. It was in Ms. Chana's opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may go along this line but there must be differences between the two, team and group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do intend to explore that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before that's done, Your Honour, this is a pleadings matter. It's a significant matter. Your Honours, it's not in the indictment, the Prosecution ought to identify where it is in the pleadings. It's not good enough to say that something arises, something is said in the open be to be tantamount to -- we are not talking -- I mean, Mr. Halilovic might be tantamount to guilty or not guilty but that won't be a verdict. "Tantamount to" is not a significant concept. Either it is or it isn't an operations group, and Your Honour, the Prosecutor has to be specific about this. Where is it in the pleadings? It can't be -- it can't just drift along in this "tantamount to" manner. We ask the Prosecutor to point where it is in the pleadings, if anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, taking into consideration of the time constraints, I believe that I would like to allow Mr. Re to continue along this line, and maybe during the cross-examination, or at a later stage, Mr. Re will furnish us with whatever is said or whatever is pled in the opening statement. Do you agree with this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think what I have to do is put on record now my objection to any questions about this. Your Honour has three options in that case. You can uphold my objection, you can reject it, or you can allow Mr. Re to proceed. My -- my submission is and I want it to be on record that I'm objecting to any more questions. I recognise there is a number of pragmatic options open to the Court, and I recognise the time situation, too, but it's a serious matter and it arises at this stage, not later, because it's not in the pleadings. And if we are now facing an operations group, rather than something tantamount to it, well, that changes the case and it changes the nature of things. So I put that on record now. I make my request that no further questions be asked about this. And I leave it to Your Honour to rule and I recognise there are a number of consideration that is you have to deal with in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there may be another option, that is we defer our rulings on this issue, but I'll let this part of the evidence to be heard in this courtroom, and later on we will decide what shall we do with this piece of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, well could I -- may I just say -- I just want to protect my position, in the sense -- I don't want to object to every question my friend asks, so could it shall taken I'm making a general objection like this. It's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic I was talking to you -- we were talking about the structure formation operations groups. We were talking about the appointment. And I was about to ask you, I think, about the structure of the command of the operations group. Was it -- did it have the same structure as all the other major units within the army? Only talking about the command structure, with all the usual assistants, assistant commanders for security or whatever.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that they had a similar, or the same, structure as another command at that level, but numerically, it's not even close, when we look at the number of people at the command of a division, which would be the same rank as an operations group, compared to the number of people that you would have in the command of an operations group. The command of an operations group most often, usually, has a certain number of people, depending on the segment to segment in the command. One to three men by each segment who make up the command. I said previously that the operations group command does not have all the other organs and services completely developed through which each command carries out the bulk of its duties. So the operations group command, the way we soldiers say it, is a miniature command in relation to some other command at that same level. For example a division command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said the appointment to an operations group was done in the same way as an appointment to other units in the army. Could an operations group be formed by the Supreme Commander, here as in Mr. Delic, or did it require a presidential -- an order of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade would be at the lowest level or -- I apologise. I started off -- from the brigade upwards to the higher levels, the brigade -- the command would form all of those, but the operative group, operations group, of course, is above the brigade. An operations group would be somewhere between the brigade and the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. My question is: Who was authorised to form or appoint an operations group? Could Mr. Delic do it or did it require an order of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, everything that happened in the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina came out of the chain of command. Therefore, General Rasim Delic, if he did form it, would form it at his proposal. He formed it. But formally, legally, the Supreme Command had to verify this with its own document, because the Supreme Command would be the one to implement this, as far as the paper work was concerned. Rasim Delic, however, would propose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could he authorise it? That's what I'm after. Could he authorise it himself or did he require presidential authorisation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. The question is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic wants to form an operations group. Can Mr. Delic, as the Supreme Commander, issue the order for it to be formed, or did he require the authorisation or approval of the Presidency to form an operations group?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now again we come to the key question, and that is the question of the relationship between the commander of the Supreme Command staff and President Izetbegovic, specifically between Rasim Delic and President Izetbegovic. He could have told him or perhaps not to form an operations group, but ultimately, this had to be covered by an official document which would have had to, and should have been, issued by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look at D146, the inspection team order of the 30th of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before that is done, it should be made very clear what is meant by the term "Supreme Command" that is found at line 22 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, by Supreme Command, what do you mean? Do you mean Mr. Delic and the staff or Mr. Izetbegovic? All I want to know is, did the president have to authorise it or could Mr. Delic do it himself? Clarify what Supreme Command means.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "the Supreme Command," I mean the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in whose composition during wartime, besides the members of the Presidency, you also had the president of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Prime Minister, I think. I'm not sure about the Minister of Defence and the commander of the Supreme Command staff. And when I say the commander of the Supreme Command, I mean the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's completely clarified. Now, look at the document, and I want you to comment on the structure in point 2 of the personnel there. I want you to comment on whether the personnel there is consistent or inconsistent with that of a -- an operations group.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to bring this into the context of an operations group or to bring the operations group into context with this. In item 2, it says that "as team leader, I appoint chief of the Main Staff, Halilovic, Sefer, and members would be representatives of the General Staff of the armed forces," and he meant -- and six names are mentioned. If I would talk about the number of people, then that would be this number 6 of six people is too few a number for a command of an operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about a smaller --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, however, go on.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the command of the operations group, and the operations group as such is something that is of a temporary nature, and this is all done at the proposal of the command -- commander of the Supreme Command Staff. So that the operations group command, if there are several such commands of several operations group, they don't have to be of the same structure because this is a temporary body. So it would depend on the commander of the Supreme Command Staff, and from the command -- Supreme Command, which approves it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you have an operations group with as few as six people appointed to the staff of it, or the command staff of it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I have to say it like that, it was not customary but everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to quickly, as quickly as we can, look at two documents which are on our list relating to a cease-fire. That's -- sorry, one document, 65 ter Exhibit 69, list. Thank you. Which is 01805268.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 391.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 391, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 17th of December 1993, an order to put in -- signed by Deputy Commander Siber, addressed to the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th Corps to the ministry of the interior relating to the London cease-fire agreement. Is that a document your corps command received?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I move that it be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I haven't got -- I apologise for this but I haven't got it on the screen yet. I'm having trouble. If the Prosecution would just excuse he me for a moment while we achieve that outcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next document I wish to show you is Prosecution 65 ter Exhibit number 28, which is 01833893.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can lend the Defence my hard copy if they want to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to that but perhaps -- perhaps if my friend wants to tender them both, perhaps he could just get an MFI number for them and we will respond in a minute when we get ourselves organised. But our screen seems to be frozen completely now, Your Honours, I'm sorry. We can't even close the things we've got open. I'm sorry, Your Honours. It may not take too long if we just don't panic, if we just take a minute. I'm sorry, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be MFI 392.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps while we are waiting, if the Prosecution can just remind me of the 65 ter number of the last document and this document. It may be that we can work that way, manually.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number for the last document is 101, and the present one is 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The LiveNote we have on the E-court is about ten pages behind the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic look at the document which should be there on the screen. It's a document dated the 26th of August 1993, under the hand of Nedzad Ajnadjic--

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- dated the 26th of August 1993 to the commander of the 1st Corps personally relating to the behaviour of the soldiers of the 10th Mountain Brigade. Did you see this document at the time, it being addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did, if I remember it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is the information in it given to you at the time about the behaviour of the 10th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. May that also be received into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you in the position to make a reply, Mr. Morrissey? If not, we could defer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, could we defer it, although that one I probably won't oppose, I must -- have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Next one could we please move to 65 ter Exhibit number 29, which is 02000095?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 28th of August 1993, under the hand of deputy commander of the Bosnian army, Jovan Divjak?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 393.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I can say without any shadow of difficulty that I'll oppose this one being tendered. Unless the witness says that he's looked at it, which might change everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me hear the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic is the document there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Have you seen this one before you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have discussions with Mr. Divjak about problems within the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you look at the document, under paragraph or point 3, it refers to the resolution of problems, "The issues and commands of the following units, delta, to my knowledge, they did not become part of the 1st Corps," close brackets, "Zulfikar, the 9th and 10th brigades, should be resolved." Now, does that reflect the content of conversations that you had with Mr. Divjak about problems within your corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Jovo Divjak was one of the deputy commanders of the Supreme Command Staff. I had many, many contacts with him. This was a topic that was discussed. He was quite often with me directly on the front lines, directly commanded units in combat and so on. So he was aware of this. I cannot specifically confirm whether on that date I talked to him, but it's quite close to this context that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next document I wish to show you -- I will move to tender it, but I understand it's objected to and we can deal with that later, if Your Honours are satisfied with that -- is 65 ter Exhibit 34 which is 01850308, which is an order of the 30th of August 1993 from the Supreme Commander to the command of the 1st Corps relating to organizational changes within the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 394.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Karavelic, is that a document you received in the course of your business as a corps commander in August or September 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the organisational changes or the proposals or the -- sorry, the directions in this order actually carried out?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I move to tender that one into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There is no opposition to that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, based upon your observations and your experiences as the 1st Corps commander and deputy commander in 1993, what did you observe about the relationship between Celo and Mr. Halilovic, and Caco and Mr. Halilovic? Taking Celo first.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what else I can say except for what has already been said through my testimony so far. That is one thing. Secondly, there were stories going around, coming from a variety of sources to the effect that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, et cetera, would go to see General Sefer Halilovic. Now, whether he did go or whether he did not go, that is something I cannot confirm. There is nothing special I can say, except for what I have already said during my testimony so far. Ramiz Delalic, Celo never addressed me in that way, and he never tried to use Sefer Halilovic as a shield or did he ever, on any occasion, in any way, defend himself by using Sefer Halilovic. No. That never happened, as far as Ramiz Delalic is concerned. Roughly, the same answer could be given as far as Caco is concerned. That is to say the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware whether Mr. Halilovic ever attended a meeting or meetings at the 9th Mountain Motorised Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it until I saw a document. I don't know how else this information could be there. A lot earlier, if not in the spring of 1993, that he was at one of the meetings at the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said you saw a document. You mean a document reporting on his attendance or something else?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was last week that I received this information. I don't know how. Perhaps I saw a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Had Mr. Halilovic attended such a meeting, what would have been the proper -- or formalities to be observed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's a leading question. There might not have been any formalities to observe and so the witness has got to establish that before it's said that he stepped outside the formal chain of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I didn't actually suggest that. I just asked what were the formalities to be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If he adds "if any," I'll be happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, if any?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Sefer Halilovic, at that time was I assume the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, the first man in the army and, as such, he does have the right to go diagonally and directly to visit units at lower levels. In terms of skipping over certain inter-levels. However, after every such meeting, it is customary, I believe in any army in the world, that after that, from that unit, or from that brigade or by the assistants who, for example, accompanied the Chief of Staff on the visit to that unit, to submit a document, a type of report, to the corps command so that the purpose of the visit and the motive of the visit would be known. However, there is another fact involved, too, that most often the chain of command is observed, and when such a visit is paid to a brigade headquarters, the corps command should know about this and the corps commander or the deputy commander or the Chief of Staff would come to attend such a meeting. However, I cannot say anything further specifically about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever see a report suggesting that Mr. Halilovic had gone to a 9th Brigade meeting? If you can answer yes or no, please do so.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you present at a meeting when -- in June 1993, when Mr. Halilovic's replacement was announced? That is, that Mr. Delic was going to be the -- was going to take a position above Mr. Halilovic in the army.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Halilovic's reaction to the news?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say that his reaction was like 99 per cent of all people would react in such a situation. Now, what am I trying to say when I say this? I'm trying to say that quite simply put, at that meeting he displayed a bit of anger because of what was being done, and because of the way things were being done. Nothing special. Basically, that it was only natural and that probably any person would react that way, if not a lot worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you say anything to him concerning his reaction to the news?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did, because after that, I think that a document was brought to that meeting by Konjicija Abdulah, an MP in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After he read this and after a brief interventions in the discussion, all of us who were present there were asked to say a few words. I think, if I manage to pair phrase my own words, I only asked General Halilovic, if I can put it that way, to calm down completely, to take this as a normal thing, let's move on, there is a war going on, and time will show, the future will show, et cetera, the correctness or incorrectness of certain steps taken by politics, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are Zakir Okovic and Sakib Okovic different people?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said in my statement meant -- was about Zakib Orovic [phoen], I did notice Sakib Okovic first in that document. I mean, I don't know a person by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is a document which I think I neglected to show you earlier, which I should have, and that's number 14 on our list, 00585517. Which is an order of the 24th of September 1993, addressed to the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade, ordering them to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 395.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Has it come up on the screen yet? You referred today earlier to sending an order to Mr. Delalic in response to Mr. Halilovic's order requesting more soldiers. Is that the order which you sent to Mr. Delalic on the 24th of September 1993? Sorry, the date on the English translation says the 24th. It should be the 23rd. No, sorry, the 24th. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I move to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could defer that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Mr. -- sorry, Karavelic, was Mr. Halilovic, to your knowledge, aware of the problems within the 9th and the 10th Brigade at the time he requested that they travel to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That question has got a number of problems with it. First of all, it has to be clear whether he's asking about this request that they travel to Jablanica early in September, the first time, or whether we are talking at a later time. Secondly, there are two different brigades, and thirdly, there is a range of different problems and rumours and stories that were floating around. And -- is this witness being asked to confirm that Halilovic knew about all of them, some of them, none of them? Which ones? That really -- so I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, but I believe that is a general question. Let's see the answer. Then if there is a necessity, Mr. Re will go into the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, when Mr. Halilovic requested the 9th and the 10th to travel to Jablanica in September 1993, early September, 1993, was he aware, to your knowledge, of the problems within the 9th and the 10th, all the problems you've testified about, or some of the problems you've testified about over the last few days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object once again. It's the use of the word "within the 9th and the 10th Brigade" that concerns me. Just about all the evidence that's been given here concerns the leaders of -- the leader of the 10th Brigade or commander of the 10th Brigade, Musan Topalovic and the deputy commander of the 9th Brigade, Ramiz Delalic. These problems within the brigade have been the subject of very little evidence over the last few days. And to put it in that -- those terms, frankly, is too broad to be meaningful and again I object to it. Because -- and the distinction I'm drawing here is within the 9th and 10th Brigade as opposed to concerning the leaders about which the evidence that is been led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution made a kind of qualification for this question. That is all the problems the witness testified about in the last few days. I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question thus qualified I would agree entirely that that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you answer that one, Mr. Karavelic? That's the state of Mr. Halilovic's knowledge, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be specific. Sefer Halilovic was in the Patriotic League. He admitted me into the Patriotic League. His headquarters were in Sarajevo. From the days of the Patriotic League, the first days of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and the siege against Sarajevo, Sefer Halilovic was incessantly in Sarajevo. His command post was in Sarajevo. As for all the political and military developments in Sarajevo he was there from day one. And in direct response to your question, I would say that as far back as in 1992, I remember very well a situation that Sefer Halilovic as Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, he had many other problems, and he knew of many other problems. When he tried to remove the commander of the 4th Brigade, Fikret Prevljak when he sent Salko Gusic as the new commander, however, he, as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, the number one man in the army, did not manage to carry this through. Now, many questions can be put why it was so. Well that is the key problem in relation to everything. He could not remove a brigade commander and he wanted to. Then, 1992, Caco and Celo, and everything concerning the 9th and 10th Brigades is something that went on over a long period of time. Caco and Celo did not come into being in September 1993. They were a consequence of what had been going on for a long time and what had not been resolved. Towards the ends of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, and the spring and summer of 1993, and so on. Deeply convinced as a soldier, as a human being, as a fellow fighter of his, that he only wanted people to defend a Bosnia-Herzegovina that was internationally recognised as an independent state. Now, why things turned out the way they did and why we are in a courtroom now is a completely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was actually asking you about the state of his knowledge. What do you know about his knowledge about the activities of the 9th and the 10th at the time that he requested parts of those units go to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command until then, and after that, at the same position, no longer the number one man of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, though, he had to know about certain activities of Caco and Celo if they actually did carry out these activities. At any rate, he could not know nearly as much as the security service knew about that. Or as much as the command of the 1st Corps knew perhaps. Let me be very specific and objective. It is the security service that knew the most. And then secondly the corps command and so on, and finally, Sefer Halilovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And finally, what was the Sandzak lobby?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, if I'd start enumerating all of them I think that there would be a countless number of lobbies. The Sandzak lobby is only one of this endless number of lobbies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was in it and what was their reputation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please. This is far too difficult a question for me. Practically, in order for me to be able to give any kind of answer to that question, that would not be serious at all. I am sorry. There is the Krajina lobby, the Drina lobby, the Eastern Bosnia lobby, the Sandzak lobby, the Albanian lobby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Witness, I believe that we heard some evidence on that Sandzak lobby already, and please concentrate on the question. Who was in it and what was their reputation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I give you the same answer that I gave to the Prosecutor. It would lack seriousness on my part to say anything about a document I first saw last week when I came here to this Court in The Hague. In one of these documents, from the security service, it says that this lobby was headed by Ejub Ganic. Throughout the war I was very close to him, and he helped me such a great deal, as an experienced politician. He helped me as a professional soldier. He fought for Bosnia-Herzegovina just as I did. I was surprised by that, but I read that. And now can I say that he was a member of the Sandzak lobby? I can't say that. Or would I say that of anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have already eight minutes past the time, and we might start this afternoon a little bit early. We'll start at 3.30 in the afternoon, and we have one hour and 30 minutes for this afternoon. Yes. The hearing for this morning is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour, as promised this morning we have had a little bit of time over lunch to sit together with the Prosecution and we would like to express our gratitude to Sureta Chana. We have now reached an agreement with the Prosecution as to quite a large number of the facts which were actually put forward as proposed adjudicated facts and it seems that Your Honours will not need to rule on this matter. We have agreed to finalising a copy of those agreed facts, which we will do in later afternoon, which will then be signed by both parties and what we propose to do is perhaps to file a new motion with those agreed facts attached to them and the Defence would then withdraw its motion on adjudicated facts so that Your Honour will not have to rule on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed for this progress. I hope that new version could be filed as early as possible and maybe -- well, we have a very busy schedule this week, I must confess. Maybe early next week? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We will undertake to do it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that Judge El Mahdi has been very kind enough to postpone his contempt case until Monday, so tomorrow afternoon, we will have some extra time to hear this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour in my opinion it's my opinion that it's possible to finish this witness tomorrow, given that extra time and that's what we hope to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karavelic. I just want to commence by asking you about the platform for the activities of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this matter -- this document has yet to be uploaded into the system, unfortunately, and so I have paper copies which will now be distributed. It may be that both English and Bosnian can be provided to the witness, whichever he wants to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I believe this document that's coming now is a document headed "the platform for the activities of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in conditions of war," and the first question is going to be, are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And can you remember how did you come to be familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had an opportunity of reading the document. I don't know when and where, but I examined it just now, because there was some military expertise in the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case that referred to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could I ask you to do, please, to point 5 of that document, which is headed "political basis of the all people's war of defence"? Do you see there in the second paragraph it provides that "patriotic forces in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, our lives together, and the ethnic equality of Muslims, Serbs and Croats, as well as members of other peoples and nationalities its, ethnic minorities, shall take part in a common multi-ethnic front." Now do you see that passage there? While you're looking, Mr. Karavelic, I'm reading from the English, but you feel free to read from whichever one suits you the best. I'm stuck with the English, frankly. Okay. Do you see that passage that I've just directed your attention to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. The next passage reads, "the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall include in their ranks members of all peoples who live in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, multi-ethnic units and commands are able to conduct the struggle for the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the aggressor with more success." And there -- there is more there. Now what I want to ask you is, what were the -- what were the implications of this presidential platform for those of you who were conducting at a higher level the actual fighting? In other words, what was the importance of the presidential platform for the army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can use one word to describe it, the greatest possible importance is what I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours could I offer that for tender, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I see no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There certainly is no objection, but I want to raise a matter on the issue of documents. Can my learned friend indicate how many documents he intends to show to the witness, because we have no idea what documents he has or where they are coming from or what size they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as for the later -- the other questions, I believe that the Defence will introduce it one by one, but at this stage, at least, Mr. Morrissey could tell the other party how many documents are you going to use or tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think this evening it's likely to be eight to ten, and I am endeavouring to slash brutally the original 60 that I had on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I ask if Mr. Morrissey would be kind enough to give us the documents we will go away and photocopy them and bring them back to court so that we are in a position to look at the documents as they are given to the witness and we, the Prosecution, are in the position to assist the Trial Chamber by being able to comment or object on the documents, if necessary, in an informed manner? Because if they are just shown to us on the screen, there is no way we can, firstly, do our job or assist the Trial Chamber especially if they are multi-page documents. I'm suggesting if Mr. Morrissey could just give us the list, we will go away and photocopy them now. And if he could just move to the documents and we will bring them back very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand that there is a motion filed by the Prosecution which is pending, and the Trial Chamber is considering the decision on that motion. We haven't come to any rulings yet at this stage. As a compromise, as a compromise, if some documents have been already admitted into the evidence, could Mr. Morrissey be kind enough to provide that list to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I can but I can't say the order in which this -- this cross-examination is going to proceed. There is a number of pressures that we have to bear at the moment. And, to be honest, I'm very reluctant to do it right now. I just started cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. But you also have a team. Maybe just write down some numbers and draw up a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would Your Honour excuse me for a moment? I'll see if I can accomplish something in short notice in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The ones which are admitted into evidence are not a problem. We have paper copies of all of those there. I can -- and I'm basically familiar with them.
