I can access them straight away. It's the new documents which we are not familiar with that are suddenly shown to a witness. The witness may well be familiar with them and we are not. We are at the greatest disadvantage in assisting the Trial Chamber because we haven't got them. It would not be difficult for Mr. Morrissey to give them -- give us the pile of documents and we could bring them back probably within ten minutes and he would have one copy and we would have the other copy. Now, in my respectful submission, that would be a very fair compromise in these circumstances. It he keeps the document he's about to use and gives us the rest, the Defence isn't photocopying them, it's not from the Defence budget we will go away and do it ourselves and we will happily assist in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I said, that there is a motion pending before us, we haven't come to any rulings at this stage. So I'm afraid that I have to repeat whatever I said, that this Bench encourages the Defence to furnish the Prosecution a list of the documents they are going to use as a good gesture. But as for there is an obligation or not, we haven't come to a decision yet. So before doing that, I'm afraid we have to follow the past practice, unless the Defence voluntarily would like to furnish that list to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The Defence declines to help now. We might consider helping at the end of the day. Right now I'm starting to cross-examine. I wish this hadn't have been sprung on me like this, and although the Chamber might take one view and the Prosecution might take another, this could have been raised at any time today. It's been raised a number of times before. To raise it right now, I don't know what the reasoning is, but I refuse to give them any such thing at the moment and I decline to help in the way suggested. But, Your Honours, what I'll do is, of course, despite the fact that we have the protection of the court's ruling, I'll give some thought to this as soon as we finish today. But we are against the clock, Your Honour, and that's why I'm very anxious to proceed if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now we were discussing the importance of this particular platform to the armed struggle and to the consequences it had for the Bosnian army. And could I just ask you this: So far as you understood your role in the war, and the role of others, officers who had been in the Patriotic League, you were determined to bring about, to fight, to protect a multi-ethnic Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to your recollection, the senior commanders that you had contact with, whether it be Sefer Halilovic, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Rasim Delic, all shared that view in the time when you were fighting, of a multi-ethnic Bosnia in which all the people would live together and fight together so long as the war lasted. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in that 100 per cent, without any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And because of that commitment to a multi-ethnic Bosnia was it an important thing for your army to try to do, and particularly the senior commanders to try to do, to ensure that no atrocities were committed on an ethnic basis against distinct ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many steps were taken, both political ones and military ones, precisely to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about the way in which the army grew into an army in a moment but there is one specific aspect of that I want to deal with now and that is following from what you just said, what steps were taken by way of giving some reality to the Geneva Conventions and giving some reality to protection of civilians by the army, in particular by the high levels of the army, in 1992 and 1993? And if you can't give an exactly exhaustive historical list from memory could you provide some examples of the sort of steps that were taken in that regard?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me now to list all the many documents, documents without force of law and with force of law, that were issued and published and to give you their titles. There were quite a number of such documents and during 1992, in actual fact, during the summer of that year, many such documents were issued, and all of them explicitly demanded absolute, 100 per cent adherence to the international Geneva Conventions on the rights of civilians and generally speaking, a wide range of rights, regardless of who they refer to, during a state of war, also respect for the provisions of international war law and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, was the same information provided at all levels of the army or was a distinction drawn between how you would explain Geneva Conventions to officers, on the one hand, and how you would explain it to the soldiers on the line on the other hand? In other words, how was it done at the different levels?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way. From top to bottom, from the Supreme Command to the last soldier in the Bosnia-Herzegovinian army, without exception to one and all. And I'm quite convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who had the job of communicating the rules to the soldiers on the line? Was that the job of you as corps commander, or was that a job that you would delegate to battalion, company commanders, having provided them with materials to help them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military hierarchy, everybody had -- was duty bound to do so towards his immediate subordinates, the superior officers to their immediate subordinates. And my task as corps commander was not to do this immediately with the soldiers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And are you able to say which level of commander at the lower levels would have the primary responsibility for telling the soldiers their obligations? Would it be a company commander or would it be at platoon level? Where would that be?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the platoon commander, the company commander and, depending on the circumstances, you might have a battalion commander involved in this. That would be the maximum top level.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt. I'm loathe to, but the question was their obligations. I'm not quite sure to what Mr. Morrissey was referring, obligations under the Geneva Conventions or obligations to -- to follow the line of hierarchy or what it is. I think that should be specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I meant obligations as this witness understood them, Your Honour. And I would submit that that's okay. But perhaps we can clarify that somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In explaining to the soldiers that they shouldn't massacre innocent civilians or behave in a bigoted or racially prejudiced way with respect to other groups, did you draw a distinction between their obligations under Bosnian law and under international law, or did you just explain to them what their duties were?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring precisely to all the positive provisions regulating on an international level this area and supported by provisions taken by the state organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the way. And so there was no distinction among the soldiers. All of them were told this in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to conclude this part of my questions, is it the fact that events like the killings at Grabovica or at Uzdol were an absolute disaster from the point of view of encouraging people to join and to fight for a multi-ethnic and tolerant Bosnia? In other words, those sort of events did not advance the war effort as you understood the war effort to be?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. And many of us experienced this as both a military and moral, and human and a catastrophe which would be against the civilians as well. So this was an enormous surprise to all of us, to all the members of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To the present day, is it possible that something like that happened and that members of the BH army did something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since you're changing the subject, I believe that if there is no objections from the Prosecution, that document you used has been admitted into the evidence and the Court Deputy will assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D396.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you and I apologise. Naturally I do have one last question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That was, at the time the Presidency passed the Presidency platform, to your understanding, Sefer Halilovic was a member of the Presidency by virtue of his office as the number one man in the army in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I now want to move on to the question of the nature of some of the units that were defending Sarajevo in 1993. And my focus in asking these questions will be on 1993, but of course if you need to refer to something earlier, you have liberty to refer to whatever is relevant, of course. Now, you indicated earlier on that the units which defended Sarajevo were not placed there had by some mobilisation plan but arose spontaneously as a result of a sudden and dangerous threat of extinction. What I want to ask is, can the same be said of the commanders of those units? Did they arise effectively out of the units themselves rather than because of some directive from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, was Musan Topalovic, Caco, one such person?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was Mujo Zulic another such person?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just so that the Tribunal knows, because we have not heard much about Mujo Zulic, which unit was Mujo Zulic the commander of? By the time we get to 1993, I mean.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the 1st Mountain Brigade, which bordered on the 10th Mountain Brigade, the left flank of the 10th mountain and the right flange of the 1st Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was Ramiz Delalic another such person?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And apart from the three that I've named, were there many other commanders who emerged from the ranks of their own unit by the will of their own soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to those units, was it a plan and a hope that the senior officers from the Patriotic League had, that one day you would bring these units into a sensible line of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I understand this is a question that is almost impossible to answer in a short way, so I'll put a proposition and you tell me if you agree or not. At the start, the collection of brave people who were fighting for Sarajevo could not really be described as an army in any military sense of the term "army." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But those of you, and I mean by these yourself, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan, Sefer Halilovic and others with JNA training, those of you who did have some expertise in military command, tried to assist the patriotic forces to organise themselves better and ultimately come to form a proper, regular army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But although it's again stating the obvious, I think it has to be stated, you didn't have time to form the army before the fighting began, did you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, throughout 1992, is it the fact that various steps were taken by way of introducing rules to introduce into the patriotic forces, elements of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely done with that goal in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I won't take you to all of these different manuals, but were the military rules and regulations of the former JNA, generally speaking, adopted as the rules of the new Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just clarify this? You mean in the original version or generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I mean generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I understand in asking these questions that I'm skating over some issues of complexity of organisation concerning the TO and other bodies, but so it will have to be. In 1992, for example, did the army under the leadership of Sefer Halilovic bring in rules governing the operation of the military security service, the SVB?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And perhaps let me ask you this: In late 1992 and into 1993, where -- to whom would a commander, an inexperienced commander who had no military training, to whom would such a commander turn to find out what the official -- Mr. Karavelic, that question has just got lost. I'm going to start it again. I apologise for that. Very well. Apart from the SVB rules that I've just referred to, were rules concerning the military police introduced?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were rules concerning the military prosecutors and military courts introduced?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it accurate to say that some units came into the line of command and control earlier than other units did?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And are you able to say whether or not the units that came into the line of command and control were generally speaking units that had senior ex-JNA officers commanding them or in their staffs? Or was there no such correlation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was precisely the case, or most often the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was Fikret Prevljak an ex-JNA person or was he one of the spontaneous commanders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that individual a bit later on. Very well. Now, considering the concrete case of Ramiz Delalic for a moment, you have indicated that despite whatever rumours or gossip there might have been about Ramiz Delalic, that at least in one respect, good can be said of him and that was he was a very brave and dedicated fighter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But for various reasons, and chiefly his refusal to cooperate with the command and control system, he came to be viewed in 1993 as a commander who the Bosnian army staff wished to remove from his command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Later on I'm going to ask you some questions about the importance of command and control and how it operates, but it's the fact, isn't it, that by 1993, Ramiz Delalic was in his place as deputy commander of the 9th Brigade not because the army command wanted him there but because his soldiers wanted him there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you might recall you were asked some questions by the learned Prosecutor earlier on as to why Ramiz Delalic wasn't simply dismissed from his post or dealt with or arrested. The reason why he wasn't simply displaced or dealt with or arrested is because to do so was likely to cause an armed conflict on the spot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And is it also the fact that some of these popular commanders recognised a common interest and were therefore potentially able to help each other if one of their number was to be arrested in that way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. That probably was the case. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I was going to put some questions to you about whether that was the case during the second of July 1993 incidents, but before I do put any such proposition I just have to clarify something. It seems from your answers that you were absent from Sarajevo and in the Igman region at the time when that incident took place; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, could you ask the witness about in which period, to be exact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: About his movements from one to the other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, no, his absence from Sarajevo, the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours could I just -- if you just bear with me for two minutes I was going to get him to give us -- well, I can do it now, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Just to anticipate something that's coming, your own position was that you came to be the deputy commander to Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan, in the 1st Corps, and could you say approximately what date you took up that office as deputy commander in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And did you remain in that post until departing for Igman in the middle of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you say approximately when it was, as near as possible to the date, when you departed to go to Igman?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first half of July, or perhaps mid-July, but I can't give you the precise date. It was thereabouts, about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you remained on Igman until sometime in August, and could you tell us when it was that you came back?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there for a month, or just over a month perhaps, so the return date is between the 10th and the 15th of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, and to clarify, your position a little further, before you left for Igman, were you formally appointed to become the commander of the 1st Corps replacing Mustafa Hajrulahovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You took up your position as commander of the 1st Corps when you returned from Igman. May I ask you, did Mustafa Hajrulahovic remain corps commander at all times up until you came back from Igman or was he acting corps commander for some period of time there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at Igman in late July 1993, I heard over the radio that I had been appointed commander of the 1st Corps, having received no prior notification whatsoever, and never having been consulted. Upon my return to Sarajevo, I was ordered to take up my duties and I obliged. In order to be quite specific about the latter part of your question, I can't be very precise about that, simply because I don't remember clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. All right. Now there are some other chronology matters that might assist here, just to put them in order, and you can confirm whether you were aware of these matters or not. You indicated that while Sefer Halilovic was still the number one man in the army -- I'm using that term because of the change in nature of the Chief of Staff office. But before the 8th of June, when Sefer was the number one in the army, you indicated in evidence that Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan, sent a request to Halilovic asking that Musan Topalovic, Caco, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and a number of other individuals be removed from their command positions and you indicated that Sefer Halilovic confirmed that document and sent it on to -- to President Izetbegovic. Now, did it have to go to President Izetbegovic because only he had the power to dismiss brigade commanders? Or only the Presidency had the power to dismiss brigade commanders or higher level commanders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only the person who appoints a brigade commander has the power to remove a brigade commander or dismiss a brigade commander, and this would be the Supreme Command, the president or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And so -- and perhaps just to take the concrete example of Fikret Prevljak, was he one of the people who -- I'm sorry, pardon me, Mr. Karavelic. Taking the concrete case of Fikret Prevljak, was he one of the individuals who Talijan, I'm sorry, who Mustafa Hajrulahovic requested be removed from his command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, and I think the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command tried to achieve precisely that. I'm not sure what was eventually achieved. Maybe the Supreme Command had blocked the move or it may have been for some other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Whatever the reason was, Fikret Prevljak remained safely in his position commanding the 4th Hrasnica brigade despite all efforts to the contrary by senior Bosnian army officers to have him removed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And indeed in the end, even though he was charged with serious criminal offences, he still survived in that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you said about serious criminal offences, I'm not sure about that. But for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, the Court proceedings that you referred to -- I'm sorry, when I said "serious criminal offences," perhaps I stated it inaccurately. I was referring to court proceedings that you yourself mentioned here so perhaps I misrepresented what you said, and I apologise if I did. Very well. Now --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand that. Yes. Okay, so now that initiative of Talijan's and Sefer Halilovic's to have those commanders removed, you've indicated that occurred early in June. Is it the fact that on the 8th of June, by a presidential order, Sefer Halilovic was replaced as the number one man in the army by Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just clarify this? The first part of your question you spoke about Fikret Prevljak and this happened in 1992, if I remember correctly, or late in 1992. There was an attempt to get him removed. On the 8th of June 1993, on the other hand, it's quite correct that General Rasim Delic became the commander of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my mistake there was caused by diverting on to the subject of Fikret Prevljak. What I really meant was that early in June 1993, plus Mustafa Hajrulahovic sent the letter concerning Topalovic, Ramiz Delalic and others, which you've indicated. Then on the 8th of June we have the removal of Halilovic from the number-one position in the army. Which you've just confirmed. And then, were you aware - you may be or you may not be - that in the middle of June, a legal opinion was given to the Presidency that the way in which the army had been restructured may have some legal difficulties and that further clarification was needed? You may know this, you may not, but I'll ask you whether you were aware of that legal opinion that happened.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I heard something about it. It does ring a bell but it's difficult for me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I'm going to come back to that. What we are doing at the moment is just establishing a chronology so some of the events make sense to the Tribunal. After that, on the 7th -- now, you're aware that there was a large offensive by the forces of the Republika Srpska which took you into battle on Igman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When did that battle -- can you put a date or an approximate date on when that battle commenced?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battle commenced much earlier. It dates back to April or May, in the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are you able --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting with Gorazde and then Trnovo and eventually Igman, including the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Both in your evidence and in other people's evidence there has been a sense of an acute crisis developing on Igman. Can you say when the crisis developed on Igman approximately?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis on Igman -- I'm not sure what specifically you have in mind but it goes back to 1992. If we are considering the period of July and August 1993 on Mount Igman, then the crisis began in the last days of July, and the situation was disastrous, over the first 10 days of August, in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And some details of that will be necessary, but later on. But just to keep the chronology going, in July, although you were absent, you did hear some news of an armed confrontation between the soldiers of Topalovic and Ramiz Delalic and certain members of the military security services and also the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Then did you become aware that on the 7th of July, Sefer Halilovic's wife was killed by a large explosion on the balcony of her flat, or of Sefer Halilovic's and her flat?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, did you have the opportunity to make contact with Sefer Halilovic in that time or were you engaged in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was engaged in combat activities throughout, for as long as I was on Igman. Sefer Halilovic came to see me on Igman. It may have been the last days of July or the first days of August. I think it was on the 5th or 6th of August that he came to Igman to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well that was going to be my next question, that -- did Sefer Halilovic can come on to Igman as part of an inspection team late in July, early in August, in order to assist you with the desperate situation you were facing at that time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of any inspection team of any kind. He came as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and he was followed by a number of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever shown the order that appointed him? I'm not suggesting you should have been but perhaps you were. So --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what order you're referring to. Appointing him to what position exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The order which sent limb on to Igman. Were you aware of whether there was an order that caused him to go to Igman and if so, did you see any such order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. I have never seen any such order. Nor am I aware of any such order being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after the first week and a half, perhaps two weeks, of August, the crisis on Igman had been controlled to some degree, is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And after that, you heard the news that Rasim Delic wanted -- or there should be summoned at Zenica a conference of corps-level commanders in order to consider future directions of the armed struggle?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commanders were summoned, corps commanders, and this all happened at the Supreme Command staff level of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me a moment, sorry, I've got a wrong note, a document here. Would you mind looking please at the Exhibit -- could the witness be shown Exhibit 219? Here comes a document that you have already seen. Can I just indicate -- thank you for providing some chronology for us, we are going to come back over some of those details now. Exhibit 219 is the appointment of a commission to consider some trench digging and taking away of civilian activities which you've already looked at in this matter. Now, just concerning the digging of trenches, it is the fact, is it not, that those trenches saved Sarajevo in a very real sense at different times? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you, Sefer Halilovic, Mustafa Hajrulahovic and other senior leaders and commanders in Sarajevo tried many, many times to get the units to get their trenches dug in the proper, legal way?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We were aware of the fact that the only way to defend our manpower from enemy missiles was just this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And manpower was all you had, really, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say it like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think you indicated you had three tanks? How many helicopters did you have?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had none. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, believe me, I don't know the exact figure, several I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several helicopters MA -- M8 helicopters. Those are helicopters used for transport. They are not combat helicopters or fighter planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thanks for that. So the document that's on the screen in front of you now which is that order establishing the commission, was just one of a number of other efforts made to regulate and to bring under control the taking of people to dig trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to show you another document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, this one is yet to be uploaded unfortunately. This is a document as signed by -- well, we'll see who it's signed by but we'll be putting it -- that it's signed by Mustafa Hajrulahovic. I just wonder if --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 397.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want you to compare this -- this document to the one that's on the screen. And what we are suggesting is that this is a document it that is a follow-up to that commission, where Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan, has attempted to assist that commission by issuing an order. Does that appear to you to be the case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this document. I've never seen it before. But there is not a shadow of a doubt that that was precisely what General Mustafa Hajrulahovic did and there is precisely what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I offer that document and -- perhaps before I do so, just -- just make this clear. By this order -- now, this was an order addressed to the 10th Mountain Brigade command proposing that that particular organ establish all necessary conditions for the work of the commission chaired by Rifat Bilajac and the other four members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And indeed, it specifies that the meeting at 1600 hours is to be attended by the 10th Brigade corps command. Do you see that at number 3?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karavelic, can I just ask you this: In a normal army, if you saw an order like that, would you draw the conclusion that since there was an order, ordering a lesser unit to meet somebody somewhere, the chances are that order would be obeyed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a normal army, yes, that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But in the Bosnian army, when you look at an order like this, the mere fact that someone issues an order has no connection to the question of whether it's going to be obeyed or not; is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to. That it's a very, very general question, asking for some speculation. My learned friend is quite entitled to ask it in relation to the 10th Brigade, given the evidence, but generally I think it's going a little bit far in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that is the Defence counsel is talking about this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can put the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Whether there order has been obeyed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I must confess my learned friend is correct in putting that I'm putting the matter more generally. He's right about that. So I'll ask the question in a different way. Because I was seeking to make a more general point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. Karavelic, sometimes the questions aren't very precise or good so I'm going to try another one. What I want to ask you is this: Just because a commander in the Bosnian army issued an order, that was no guarantee that it was going to be obeyed; is that correct, as a general proposition at this time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in particular, when issuing orders to the 9th Brigade or to the 10th Brigade, it was a question of the will -- I'll withdraw that. I'm going to put that question nor precisely. You as a deputy commander and ultimately a commander could issue orders to these units but in real terms, it was a matter of their choice whether they obeyed or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, frequently, but if you're speaking specifically, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sometimes the 10th Brigade did, in fact, appear to comply with an order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And sometimes the 9th Brigade would appear to have complied with an order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But you couldn't conclude from that fact that either of them was in the line of command and control, could you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Because when a unit obeys orders when it feels like it, it's not in the line of command and control, is it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that it isn't, but I can put it differently and say not completely, not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, just moving forward for a moment to another -- sorry, perhaps, yes, there is one other document I'd like to show. I offer that document for tender. Did I do that already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, subject, of course, to some information on its provenance, its chain of custody, how the Defence got it, and how it came to be before the Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me a moment, please. I'll ask those who know better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we go into the private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D397.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were two documents provided by that individual on request by the Defence, and now I turn to the next of those. Could the witness please be shown -- this is Defence 65 ter number D1550. Again it's not uploaded as a hard copy yet but of course will be in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 398.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The document that's coming now is on the face of it a report by Bilajac, Maslak, Komad [phoen], Kinja [phoen], and Hasinovic. I just wonder if you wouldn't minds taking a moment to look at that document, and as you're doing so would you just note the order number at the top there? In particular, what I'm going to ask you about is the recommendations. Mr. Karavelic, you can indicate when you're finished reading that and --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. There is just two parts I want to draw your attention to. The first is the recommendations there. It's recommended that Musan Topalovic, also known as Caco, be relieved of duty. That's not the first time that a recommendation was made to remove Musan Topalovic from duty, is it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the second thing I wanted to take you to was -- back in paragraph number 2, you can see that there is a reference to a previous order dated the 25th of December 1992, prohibiting the unauthorised bringing in and take of citizens.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prohibiting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in short, this is -- this document, to your knowledge, is just one of a long line of efforts made to bring the trench-digging problem under control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I offer that document for tender as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think my learned colleague asked the witness whether he'd ever seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thought I had, Your Honour, but I apologise if I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. At least I don't remember having seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At all events, does it appear to you to be entirely consist tends with the two other documents that you were shown, namely the commission of the 3rd of June 1993 and the order of the 5th of June 1993 and indeed to be a report by that very commission?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And finally, it may be -- you may be able to remember, although I know it's 11 years later, but if you wouldn't mind just looking at the signature on the other side, you might confirm whether you're now in a position to say that you recognise the signature of Rifat Bilajac or Enver Maslak?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only signature that I used to see more was Rifat Bilajac and Maslak, Enver. Those two signatures. I think those are the signatures but of course I can't say 100 per cent, just as like I -- just as I wouldn't be able to say for any other signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, us I do offer it for tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D398.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, arising from that little sequence of documents, we know -- well, perhaps -- I'll just put the question as a cross examining question. Musan Topalovic despite that report, was not removed from his commanding post at the 10th Brigade at that time, was he?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to list a couple of reasons why it wasn't appropriate to use force against Musan Topalovic or indeed against Ramiz Delalic at that time, and I'll get to you comment on each one as I raise it. First of all, if the SVB, military security service, and any military police with them, went to arrest either of the two individuals, Delalic or Topalovic, the -- there was a high likelihood of armed conflict with -- between those military police and the local units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And this -- any such conflict had a number of bad effects. First of all, it might result in significant numbers of casualties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Secondly, it could be very damaging for army morale more generally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thirdly, it might provide a specific military opportunity for the Republika Srpska forces when such a conflict was going on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And fourthly, there was in the middle of 1993 some level of tension and distrust in some parts of the front between the fighting front line soldiers on the one hand and the MUP policemen on the other hand, whatever the reasons might be; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And triggering a conflict by going to arrest Ramiz Delalic or Musan Topalovic was something that might have very far-reaching consequences in terms of civil strife in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And finally, there was a danger that if a confrontation took place between security organs on the one hand and units of Delalic or Topalovic on the other hand, that other units might take the decision to join in or contribute to such a conflict. Was that a danger?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just add something, the key problem was that this applied to both sides, and you are entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking to you enter a judgement on who was right and wrong about this question, but what was the grievance, if you like, that the army soldiers had against the MUP, the military police? And by "army soldiers," I mean the soldiers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, people used to say that those were Baba's sons or fashion models. They had everything. They had very fancy uniforms, nice boots, good weapons, sufficient ammunition. And that on the other hand, their total contribution to the Defence of Sarajevo was quite inadequate. They were called "daddy's little boys" for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And at a higher level in the army, did some of you, and I'm perhaps talking of people at the level that were you at and at the corps level with Mustafa Hajrulahovic and others, and perhaps also staff members such as Mr. Bilajac, Mr. Suljevic, Mr. Karic, and that level of people, was there a shared feeling there that there needed to be more coordination and more cooperation in military matters between the army and the forces of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just excuse me, please, one moment. There is a document I'd like to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I clarify something? The question -- the two questions back, my learned friend said "grievance, if you like, the army soldiers had against the MUP, the military police." I'm not sure whether the witness's answer was referring to the military police or to the MUP. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. Of course it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't know if you understood the objection there. But there has been a request for a clarification about whether the soldiers on the ground -- I'll ask the question another way. When you were talking about the daddy's boys there, were you talking about the civilian police, the MUP, or the military police, or both?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian police, or the MUP, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, there is a -- just have to excuse me a moment, sorry. There is a document I want to go to now and I just have to turn it up. Okay. Before I come to this document I just want a couple of other general questions to ask. With respect to the -- the need for there to be further coordination between the MUP forces and the army forces, do you recall Sefer Halilovic making it clear on a number of occasions, one of which I'll put to you in a minute, that he thought that the extensive human and material and technical potential of the MUP for war tasks and duties ought to be mobilised to a much greater extent than it was currently being? In other words, did you understand that to be Sefer's position in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I know that. And that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not there was a proposal made -- I'm just going to show you a document now. Just excuse me one moment, please. Pardon me, I'm sorry about that. This document is uploaded. This is Defence 65 ter number DD000198. Sorry, 65 ter number D52 and it's DD000198.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 399.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I might have provided the wrong number there. It's DD00-0195. My apologies for that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The document that's going to be shown to you now is the document under the name of Sefer Halilovic, chief of the SVK of the Bosnian army. It's dated Sarajevo, 27 May 1993. So it's maybe a bit over a week before he was removed from his position as the number one man in the army. Now, this is a document that you may have seen before you may not, and you might need to read the whole thing to find out. If you look at it and tell us that you've read it before, please tell us, otherwise just take your time to read it and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We don't have there document. I've just tried to find it on the screen but it's come up saying you are not authorised to view there one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That was the plan. Your Honour, I'm sorry about that. It should be released. I think it's released now, is it? I'm told it's released, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We saw it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a four-page document we have not seen before. I cannot deal with that document on this screen and attempt to look at a -- the transcript a metre away. I physically can't do it. I really need a paper copy. I cannot do my job trying to look at a four-page document, scrolling through it while the transcript is a metre away. I just can't do it. So I really request a paper copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's going to be provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the witness might just do the very best he can to read it on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've finished the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As you read, I just draw your attention to a matter that I want to ask you a question about. You'll see in about the middle of the document that there is a call made by Mr. Halilovic that -- and I'm quoting, "the substantial military potential of the MUP is placed under a single command."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which page is this in the English, page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In the English it's page DD000200 and it's at the top, perhaps about four lines down. Your Honours, while the witness is looking at that might I mention a very brief housekeeping matter? In situations like this, I certainly understand my learned friend's position about a document that's got some more pages to it. Just because of the way things have unfolded with this witness we are rushing here and I acknowledge that's the sort of document I would like to have given him and perhaps if we had a bit more time. I understand we outmatch the Prosecution in resources overwhelmingly, but, anyway, we just weren't quite able to get there. But I did notice the possibility of printing a document in court. I don't know if that's something that the Court is able to discuss with us in future because sometimes if a paper copy were needed in a hurry, if the Court were able to print one, that can help and it certainly can -- my learned friend today showed a paper copy to a witness which helped and that may be a pragmatic thing that we can do in the future. I just mention it now. I'm not saying that the Court has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that's a very good suggestion. Maybe each party's table will be furnished with a printer so whatever document they lack they could print it out on the spot rather than going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, sorry, Mr. Karavelic, I understand I've given you a lengthy document at short notice here. What's the progress report? Are we nearly finished or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished reading the part that talks about the civilian police and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, look I just want to confirm this. First of all, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really confirm, but the substance is very familiar. I believe it tallies with what I've read so far with the document. The conclusion is either I'm familiar with the document or I actually read it at some point, but I don't remember it exactly when. Or if I did at all. However, as to the substance, I can confirm everything the document appears to say, and I think it's safe to assume the same in relation to what I have not read. I was familiar with this at the time. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D399.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do Your Honours propose to sit on -- any further on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm not in a position to do so because the time allocated to us for today is over. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours play I just say I think the learned Prosecutor and I would both agree in thanking the Court staff who have helped to do these long hours and so on. Your Honours, can I indicate that I think we will finish this witness tomorrow. I expect to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. So the hearing for today is adjourned. We'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.
